query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In pre-exposed Q235 steel, the nanoscale heterogeneity of the residual pickling/passivation film – specifically the uneven distribution of residual fluorine and nitrogen species versus in situ–formed iron oxides – governs whether the film will uniformly transform into a protective barrier or develop localized weaknesses that permit chloride penetration and rapid corrosion. A controlled brief annealing treatment that promotes a more uniform conversion to iron oxide will improve corrosion resistance under both room‐temperature atmospheric (salt spray) and high‐temperature simulated concrete pore conditions relative to unannealed, pre-exposed samples.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 low‐carbon steel in its pre‐exposure state after standard pickling and passivation (with a dense dark black film containing elevated F and N on the surface)
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, brief annealing treatment designed to promote uniform transformation of residual passivation species into a consistent iron oxide layer (and diminish remnant F/N heterogeneity) versus leaving the sample unannealed
generation.conditions: Evaluate both under cyclic salt spray exposure at room temperature (simulating chloride‐driven pitting scenarios) and under high-temperature simulated concrete pore solution conditions (where accelerated passivation is indicated by temperature) while keeping other environmental parameters constant
generation.structural_mediator: The density, uniformity, and chemical composition (iron oxide-dominant vs. heterogeneous residual F/N areas) of the passive film
generation.mechanism: In the untreated (heterogeneous) state, regions retaining residual passivation species (F/N) act as weak spots where chloride ions can more easily penetrate and disrupt the film, accelerating localized corrosion. Annealing induces a uniform conversion to a stable, thicker iron oxide layer with improved charge transfer resistance, thereby retarding film rupture and corrosion progression.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will exhibit lower weight loss, higher impedance values in EIS, fewer and smaller localized pitting events (as observed by SEM and XPS), indicating a more homogeneous and protective passive film in both room temperature and high-temperature conditions compared to unannealed samples
generation.baseline: Pre-exposed Q235 steel samples produced by standard pickling/passivation without any further thermal treatment
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to pre‐exposed Q235 steel where the passivation film’s initial chemistry from pickling (high F/N residues) is present; it may not hold in cases where alternative inhibitor films (e.g., organic adsorption layers) or additional surface modifications (HEA cladding) dominate the corrosion behavior
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends the observations of film breakdown and weight loss kinetics in atmospheric salt spray from PMC9504384::web::028::4_conclusions and the enhanced, temperature‐accelerated uniform passivation in SCP solutions from PMC9867134::web::023::4_conclusions to propose that controlled thermal treatment can reconcile the conflicting roles of temperature on passivation film integrity; however, the exact transformation kinetics and quantitative effects remain to be determined

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples from identical pickled/passivated pre-exposed stocks. Subject one set to a brief annealing treatment at a controlled temperature (e.g., 250–300 °C for a short time) designed to promote uniform oxide conversion, while keeping the other set as control. Expose both sets to a cyclic salt spray test (room temperature, e.g., for 12 days) and a high-temperature simulated concrete pore solution test (e.g., at 60 °C for 24 hours). Analyze surface film chemistry (using XPS), morphology (using SEM), EIS response, and weight loss.
measurements: XPS to determine the uniformity and composition of the passive film (Fe oxide content vs. residual F/N content)
SEM imaging to assess localized pitting and film rupture
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to quantify film resistance
Weight loss measurements for corrosion kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., higher film impedance, lower weight loss, fewer pitting sites) over the unannealed controls under both test conditions, or if the unannealed samples perform better, then the hypothesis linking film uniformity (via transformation induced by annealing) to improved corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, the corrosion behavior and mechanism of Q235 in atmospheric environment are studied by designing a cyclic salt spray accelerated corrosion experiment. The specific conclusions are as follows: Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of the accelerated corrosion process can be roughly divided into four stages: (1) passivation film corrosion product generation and local shedding, (2) matrix rust layer generation and covering, (3) rust layer accumulation and stacking onto a flat and dense second protective layer, and (4) matrix rust layer breaking through the protective layer continues to grow thicker until shedding. After pickling passivation treatment of Q235 low-carbon steel in the atmospheric environment of corrosion from passivation film weakness, pitting corrosion gradually develops into comprehensive corrosion with the elongation of time. Rust layer composition gradually transitions from passivation products into iron oxide based on hydroxyl iron oxide. The whole process is “from point to surface” corrosion. In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.
